title: Astronomy — Pictor Nebula
prompt:
Listen to an audio passage, answer all multiple-select questions, then rate passage and question difficulty.

This is the stimuli:
Transcript:
About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. The colors and shapes seem almost too vivid to be real, though they're exactly what the telescope captures. It's the kind of sight that makes clear why so many people find deep-sky objects captivating.

Questions:
Question 1: Which of the following correctly describe the Pictor Nebula? Select all that apply. 1) It is a cloud of gas 2) It is located about four thousand light-years from Earth 3) It is lit from within by young stars 4) It is a dense ball of old stars 5) None of the above
Question 2: How do scientists observe the Pictor Nebula? Select all that apply. 1) With an optical telescope 2) By picking up red light emitted by the nebula 3) Using radio equipment that picks up regular pulses 4) By measuring how its mass varies over time 5) None of the above
Question 3: What do astronomers study the Pictor Nebula to learn? Select all that apply. 1) How gravity pulls pockets of gas together 2) How gas clouds ignite into new stars 3) How gravitational waves ripple through a region of space 4) How black hole emissions change 5) None of the above
Question 4: Which of the following correctly describes the Pictor Nebula? Select all that apply. 1) A gas cloud lit by embedded young stars that is studied to understand how new stars form 2) A gas cloud lit by embedded young stars that is studied to understand gravitational waves 3) The remains of a dying star that is studied to understand how new stars form 4) The remains of a dying star that is studied to understand gravitational waves 5) None of the above
Question 5: Which of the following correctly identifies what the Pictor Nebula is? Select all that apply. 1) An emission nebula — a dense ball of old stars gravitationally bound together 2) A globular pulsar — a cloud of gas lit by its own embedded young stars 3) A globular pulsar — the collapsed core of an exploded massive star 4) An emission nebula — two stars in a close gravitational orbit 5) None of the above

On a scale 1-10, rate how difficult the passage was, and how difficult the questions were.

Give your response according to the following formatting rules:
Output ONLY lines in this exact format:
Question 1: 1,3
Question 2: 2
...
Passage Difficulty: 7
Question Difficulty: 7
(List every correct option number for a question, separated by commas. If none apply, use the "None of the above" option number.)

Question 1: 1,2,3
Question 2: 1,2

Transcript:
About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. The colors and shapes seem almost too vivid to be real, though they're exactly what the telescope captures. It's the kind of sight that makes clear why so many people find deep-sky objects captivating.

Questions:

Question 2: How do scientists observe the Pictor Nebula? Select all that apply. 1) With an optical telescope 2) By picking up red light emitted by the nebula 3) Using radio equipment that picks up regular pulses 4) By measuring how its mass varies over time 5) None of the above
Question 3: What do astronomers study the Pictor Nebula to learn? Select all that apply. 1) How gravity pulls pockets of gas together 2) How gas clouds ignite into new stars 3) How gravitational waves ripple through a region of space 4) How black hole emissions change 5) None of the above
Question 4: Which of the following correctly describes the Pictor Nebula? Select all that apply. 1) A gas cloud lit by embedded young stars that is studied to understand how new stars form 2) A gas cloud lit by embedded young stars that is studied to understand gravitational waves 3) The remains of a dying star that is studied to understand how new stars form 4) The remains of a dying star that is studied to understand gravitational waves 5) None of the above
Question 5: Which of the following correctly identifies what the Pictor Nebula is? Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Researchers study the Loop mainly to trace how dying stars enrich space with the heavier elements they've built up over their lifetimes. About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

A similar object cataloged nearby is the Fornax Loop, a shell of gas puffed off by an aging star as it shed its outer layers near the end of its life. Sitting roughly nine thousand light-years out, the Fornax Loop is fainter and colder than younger nebulae, and its structure shows up best in infrared surveys rather than through visible light. Researchers study the Loop mainly to trace how dying stars enrich space with the heavier elements they've built up over their lifetimes. Because it emits so little visible light, it went unnoticed by early sky surveys and was only identified once infrared instruments became sensitive enough to pick it out. Spectroscopic analysis shows elevated carbon and nitrogen relative to hydrogen, consistent with material dredged up from the star's core in its final years. The shell is expanding outward at roughly twelve kilometers per second, slow enough that it should fully disperse within about ten thousand years.

Transcript:
About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

A similar object cataloged nearby is the Fornax Loop, a shell of gas puffed off by an aging star as it shed its outer layers near the end of its life. Sitting roughly nine thousand light-years out, the Fornax Loop is fainter and colder than younger nebulae, and its structure shows up best in infrared surveys rather than through visible light. Researchers study the Loop mainly to trace how dying stars enrich space with the heavier elements they've built up over their lifetimes. Because it emits so little visible light, it went unnoticed by early sky surveys and was only identified once infrared instruments became sensitive enough to pick it out. Spectroscopic analysis shows elevated carbon and nitrogen relative to hydrogen, consistent with material dredged up from the star's core in its final years. The shell is expanding outward at roughly twelve kilometers per second, slow enough that it should fully disperse within about ten thousand years.

Question 2: Which of the following are true of how Bracklin is woven? Question 5: Which of the following correctly describes a feature of bracklin? Transcript:
Bracklin is a textile made exclusively from the fleece of the Grennock mountain sheep. Every bolt of Bracklin traces back to the same source: fleece sheared from the particular breed of mountain sheep that live in the highlands of Grennock. Grennock mountain sheep fleece makes particularly warm fabrics.

Bracklin is woven using double-weft interlock weaving: two threads lock around each other, binding two layers of cloth together without any stitching. That locking — not crossing — is why double-weft interlock weaving keeps its layers bound tight. No extra thread is needed — double-weft interlock weaving holds itself together.

The cloth is used mainly for winter outerwear and ceremonial robes. Those are bracklin's two main uses — winter outerwear and ceremonial robes, nothing else. Both draw on the same warmth, just for different occasions.

Before it is dyed, bracklin fabric ranges from warm ivory to ash grey. That ivory-to-grey range comes straight from the sheep's own coat. Pale ivory bolts are rarest; most fleece runs closer to ash-grey.

Questions:
Question 1: Which of the following are true of Bracklin? Select all that apply. 1) It is made out of sheep's wool 2) It can be made out of the wool of Grennock mountain sheep 3) It can be made out of the wool of any type of sheep 4) It can be made out of the wool of Cheshire mountain sheep 5) None of the above
Question 2: Which of the following are true of how Bracklin is woven? Select all that apply. 1) Two threads lock around each other during weaving 2) The interlocking binds two layers of cloth together without any stitching 3) Three threads are braided together tightly 4) The layers are bound together afterward with hand-stitching 5) None of the above

Transcript:
Bracklin is a textile made exclusively from the fleece of the Grennock mountain sheep. Every bolt of Bracklin traces back to the same source: fleece sheared from the particular breed of mountain sheep that live in the highlands of Grennock. Grennock mountain sheep fleece makes particularly warm fabrics.

Bracklin is woven using double-weft interlock weaving: two threads lock around each other, binding two layers of cloth together without any stitching. That locking — not crossing — is why double-weft interlock weaving keeps its layers bound tight. No extra thread is needed — double-weft interlock weaving holds itself together.

The cloth is used mainly for winter outerwear and ceremonial robes. Those are bracklin's two main uses — winter outerwear and ceremonial robes, nothing else. Both draw on the same warmth, just for different occasions.

Transcript:
The Mirelon is a fruit with deep indigo-black skin covered in a white powdery bloom. Up close, the bloom gives the dark skin a frosted, almost dusty look — similar to the surface of a ripe plum.

Its flesh is a vivid saffron-yellow due to a pigment called nivellin. Nivellin is what gives the mirelon its signature yellow color. 

The mirelon's botanical name is Thyrsocarpus niveus. Thyrsocarpus niveus is the mirelon's official scientific name.

Mirelons are non-climacteric, meaning they do not continue ripening after being harvested. Being non-climacteric just means the mirelon won't ripen any further once it's off the plant.

Mirelons grow at elevations between 900 to 4000 feet above sea level. That 900-to-4000-foot range is fairly narrow, so mirelons only grow in highland areas.

Questions:
Question 1: Which of the following correctly describe the outer appearance of the Mirelon? Select all that apply. 1) The skin is a dark, nearly black shade of blue 2) The skin is dusted with a pale white powdery coating 3) The skin is a warm yellow color 4) The surface is smooth and glossy 5) None of the above
Question 2: Which of the following are true of the Mirelon's flesh? Select all that apply. 1) The interior is a warm, deep golden-yellow 2) The color of the flesh comes from a pigment called nivellin 3) The interior is a soft pale violet 4) The color of the flesh comes from a pigment called thornellin 5) None of the above
Question 3: What is the botanical name of the Mirelon? Select all that apply. 1) Thyrsocarpus niveus 2) Thyrsocarpus pallens 3) Spinofex arbens 4) Thyrsocarpus mirabilis 5) None of the above
Question 4: Which combination correctly describes the Mirelon? 1) Does not continue ripening once harvested; grows above 900 feet 2) Does not continue ripening once harvested; grows below 500 feet 3) Continues ripening after harvest; grows above 900 feet 4) Continues ripening after harvest; grows below 500 feet 5) None of the above
Question 5: Which of the following correctly describes a mirelon's feature? Select all that apply. 1) Its outer skin is pale yellow with fine raised bristles 2) Its flesh is colored by a compound called shortellin 3) It is a climacteric fruit that continues ripening after harvest 4) Its botanical name Thyrsocarpus rufa 5) None of the above

Listen to an audio passage, answer all multiple-select questions, then rate passage and question difficulty.

This is the stimuli:
Transcript:
The Mirelon is a fruit with deep indigo-black skin covered in a white powdery bloom. Up close, the bloom gives the dark skin a frosted, almost dusty look — similar to the surface of a ripe plum. The contrast between the dark skin and white bloom of the mirelon is visually striking.

Its flesh is a vivid saffron-yellow due to a pigment called nivellin. Nivellin is what gives the mirelon its signature yellow color. Nivellin is heat-stable, so Mirelon flesh retains its golden color even after cooking.

The mirelon's botanical name is Thyrsocarpus niveus. Thyrsocarpus niveus is the mirelon's official scientific name. Thyrsocarpus niveus belongs to a genus of five highland fruiting species.

Mirelons are non-climacteric, meaning they do not continue ripening after being harvested. Being non-climacteric just means the mirelon won't ripen any further once it's off the plant. Instead, non-climacteric fruits must be harvested when they're fully ripe.

Mirelons grow at elevations between 900 to 4000 feet above sea level. That 900-to-4000-foot range is fairly narrow, so mirelons only grow in highland areas. No planting below 900 feet has ever produced a reliable harvest.

Questions:
Question 1: Which of the following correctly describe the outer appearance of the Mirelon? Select all that apply. 1) The skin is a dark, nearly black shade of blue 2) The skin is dusted with a pale white powdery coating 3) The skin is a warm yellow color 4) The surface is smooth and glossy 5) None of the above
Question 2: Which of the following are true of the Mirelon's flesh? Select all that apply. 1) The interior is a warm, deep golden-yellow 2) The color of the flesh comes from a pigment called nivellin 3) The interior is a soft pale violet 4) The color of the flesh comes from a pigment called thornellin 5) None of the above
Question 3: What is the botanical name of the Mirelon? Select all that apply. 1) Thyrsocarpus niveus 2) Thyrsocarpus pallens 3) Spinofex arbens 4) Thyrsocarpus mirabilis 5) None of the above
Question 4: Which combination correctly describes the Mirelon? 1) Does not continue ripening once harvested; grows above 900 feet 2) Does not continue ripening once harvested; grows below 500 feet 3) Continues ripening after harvest; grows above 900 feet 4) Continues ripening after harvest; grows below 500 feet 5) None of the above
Question 5: Which of the following correctly describes a mirelon's feature? Select all that apply. 1) Its outer skin is pale yellow with fine raised bristles 2) Its flesh is colored by a compound called shortellin 3) It is a climacteric fruit that continues ripening after harvest 4) Its botanical name Thyrsocarpus rufa 5) None of the above

Mirelons grow at elevations between 900 to 4000 feet above sea level. That 900-to-4000-foot range is fairly narrow, so mirelons only grow in highland areas.

Transcript:
The Mirelon is a fruit with deep indigo-black skin covered in a white powdery bloom. Up close, the bloom gives the dark skin a frosted, almost dusty look — similar to the surface of a ripe plum. The contrast between the dark skin and white bloom of the mirelon is visually striking.

Its flesh is a vivid saffron-yellow due to a pigment called nivellin. Nivellin is what gives the mirelon its signature yellow color. Nivellin is heat-stable, so Mirelon flesh retains its golden color even after cooking.

The mirelon's botanical name is Thyrsocarpus niveus. Thyrsocarpus niveus is the mirelon's official scientific name. Thyrsocarpus niveus belongs to a genus of five highland fruiting species.

Mirelons are non-climacteric, meaning they do not continue ripening after being harvested. Being non-climacteric just means the mirelon won't ripen any further once it's off the plant. Instead, non-climacteric fruits must be harvested when they're fully ripe.

Mirelons grow at elevations between 900 to 4000 feet above sea level. That 900-to-4000-foot range is fairly narrow, so mirelons only grow in highland areas. No planting below 900 feet has ever produced a reliable harvest.

Listen to an audio passage, answer all multiple-select questions, then rate passage and question difficulty.

This is the stimuli:
Transcript:
Velthrak is a grappling art where striking of any kind is not permitted. Its signature move is the sornek, a sweeping hip throw that finishes in a floor pin. Full-resistance sparring is off-limits for anyone with under two years of experience. Originating in the Dalviri Highlands, velthrak is governed by the Dalviri Arts Council, which was founded in 1947.

A related striking art from a neighboring region is kestro, built around punches, kicks, and elbow strikes rather than throws. Bouts are scored on a ten-point system: a clean strike to the torso earns two points, a strike to the head earns three, and a knockdown scores a full five, with judges deducting a point for any strike below the waist. Fighters are classified into five weight tiers, and each tier has its own minimum number of sanctioned bouts required before a fighter can be ranked nationally. Matches run three rounds of two minutes each, separated by a mandatory ninety-second rest interval. Judges score each bout independently and submit tallies to a central scoring table, where a majority-decision rule resolves any split verdict among the three officials.

Questions:
Question 1: Which of the following accurately describe the style of velthrak? Select all that apply. 1) Velthrak is a grappling-focused art 2) Velthrak does not permit striking of any kind 3) Velthrak is a striking-focused art 4) Velthrak allows limited strikes during competition 5) None of the above
Question 2: Which of the following accurately describe the sornek? Select all that apply. 1) It is the signature technique of velthrak 2) It involves a hip throw 3) It starts with a spinning elbow strike to the opponent's shoulder 4) It begins with a leg pick 5) None of the above
Question 3: Which of the following correctly describes the governing body of velthrak? Select all that apply. 1) The Dalviri Arts Council governs velthrak certification 2) The official governing body of velthrak was formed in 1967 3) The official governing body of velthrak was formed in 1947 4) The Dalviri Federation of Combat Arts governs velthrak certification 5) None of the above
Question 4: Which of the following correctly describes velthrak? Select all that apply. 1) Full-resistance sparring involves kicking and punching 2) Practitioners must complete 200 strikes on a bag before each session 3) Practitioners must practice for three years before engaging in full-resistance sparring 4) Practitioners must practice for two years before engaging in full-resistance sparring 5) None of the above
Question 5: Which of the following are restrictions that apply in velthrak? Select all that apply. 1) Striking an opponent in any form is against the rules 2) A person who has practiced velthrak for one year cannot engage in full-resistance sparring 3) The sornek may only be performed in championship-level bouts 4) All competition surfaces must be approved by the Dalviri Federation of Combat Arts 5) None of the above
